questions.q: What does the no-cloning theorem state precisely?
options: Quantum states can be cloned, but only if they are in superposition
Qubits can never be measured more than once
Classical bits cannot be copied either, under any circumstances
No physical process can produce two independent copies of an arbitrary unknown quantum state while leaving the original intact
questions.explain: No-cloning forbids a universal copying process for arbitrary unknown states -- it says nothing about known states, which can always be prepared repeatedly.

questions.q: Why is no-cloning a fundamental mathematical result rather than an engineering limitation?
options: It is simply a rule imposed by convention in quantum computing textbooks
It follows directly from the linearity of quantum evolution: a cloning machine that works on basis states provably fails on superpositions of them
It only applies to qubits built from superconducting circuits
It has never actually been proven, only assumed
questions.explain: Because quantum evolution must be linear, any hypothetical universal cloning machine can be shown to fail on superposition inputs -- this is a mathematical consequence, not a hardware gap that better engineering could close.

questions.q: A lab prepares 100 identical copies of the state |0>, which they know in advance. Does this violate no-cloning?
options: Yes, unless the copies are entangled with each other
No -- no-cloning only forbids copying an arbitrary unknown state; preparing many copies of a known state is always allowed
Yes -- any process producing multiple copies of any quantum state violates no-cloning
No, but only if the copies are never measured
questions.explain: No-cloning specifically targets unknown states carrying information you don't already have; repeated preparation of a known state is unrelated to the theorem.

questions.q: Why does the classical repetition code's 'make 3 copies, then vote' trick fail directly because of no-cloning?
options: The repetition code depends on being able to copy the bit/state being protected, which is exactly what no-cloning forbids for an unknown qubit state
The repetition code fails only because qubits decohere, unrelated to cloning
Majority vote itself is mathematically undefined for quantum states
No-cloning has nothing to do with the repetition code's failure in the quantum setting
questions.explain: The repetition scheme's core assumption -- that you can freely copy the thing being protected -- is precisely the assumption no-cloning removes for an unknown quantum state.

questions.q: How do real quantum codes achieve redundancy without violating no-cloning?
options: They don't -- quantum error correction is only theoretical and has never been implemented
By measuring the logical qubit directly and writing the result onto several other qubits
By spreading the logical qubit's information across several physical qubits via entanglement, rather than producing literal copies of the logical state
By cloning the qubit just before any error can occur, then discarding the clone afterward
questions.explain: Encoding circuits entangle the physical qubits so the logical information is distributed across their correlations, with no single qubit or literal copy ever holding the full logical state -- this is how no-cloning is respected.
